Source: Paul's addendum "Melange Annotated Bibliography — Addendum" (sha12 d09295bf5960), read in full (68 lines). The companion reviewer-annotation file _annots/d09295bf5960.json does not exist, so there are no reviewer comments or highlights to add. Entries are Paul's own annotations paraphrased, and citations are recorded as he wrote them; I did not verify them externally.

Overarching argument: the section extends the static influence-maximization entries (Kempe et al. 2003; Nemhauser-Wolsey-Fisher 1978, covered elsewhere) into a dynamic regime organized in three tiers that mirror the Melange architecture. Tier 1 is one-shot greedy, which is static and submodular and gives the 1-1/e (about 63%) bound. Tier 2 is adaptive greedy, the bridge: a subordinate routine that replans within a campaign as intelligence arrives, with a survival guarantee (Golovin-Krause; CELF makes it computationally practical). Tier 3 is the RL envelope, where a learned outer policy handles cross-campaign compounding, where no greedy guarantee reaches.

Unifying claim: the inner static problem is submodular, the inner sequential problem is adaptive submodular, and the full cross-campaign problem is non-submodular. Paul asserts that RL4CCIM confirms the last point for complex contagion, and that the non-submodular regime is where the durable competitive moat lives.

Systems linked: the operational layer (D* Lite / LPA*, incremental replanning) maps to adaptive submodularity; the strategic layer (MCTS and the orienteering "reach-while-collecting" frame) maps to the RL-IM sequential, long-horizon problem; the political-capital budget maps to GCOMB's budget constraint; the subordinate greedy routine feeds the outer MDP through marginal-influence shaping rewards.

Research questions and implicit hypotheses: (a) whether coalition formation in Congress is a complex contagion (a fence-sitter commits only once enough allies have), which Paul calls "plausibly" true and which would place Melange outside the submodular regime; (b) whether relationship and persuasion costs, unknown a priori, can be learned by probing (Kamarthi); (c) whether lobbying commitment that is probabilistic rather than guaranteed (Chen 2021) changes the seeding policy.

Stated gaps and caveats in the addendum: adaptive submodularity presumes exact expected spread, which is NP-hard in general, and this is the stated reason Paul still drifts toward learned methods. The frontier paragraph says the four anchored RL entries are "sufficient"; the section in fact anchors seven RL-IM entries plus foundations, so that sentence is loosely worded. The frontier work (MaDGNN) is named without authors or DOI and is not anchored. The Golovin entry's "first to study influence maximization under the adaptive model" is Paul's priority claim and is unverified here.

Overarching arguments and design rulings:
- Layering: the member layer (cosponsorship and press) stays independent. The staffer network is its own layer below members, with members as attachment points and no member-member edges. Lobbyists enter as outsiders via revolving-door edges. Layers combine only at analysis time in a multiplex, never inside each other's weights. Multiplying the cosponsorship adjacency into staffer weights is banned as double-counting and as a comparability contaminant (same failure class as the LD-2 circularity).
- Edge rule (OVERLAP): a person-person edge requires real temporal overlap in the same container, weighted by overlap duration times container kappa. Sequence across offices is a trajectory property (ordered stints, office-to-office moves), never a person-person edge. Every build must emit a negative control counting edges a build without the overlap test would produce.
- Education is excluded (weight alpha=0 kept in code), so the final weight reduces to W = w_work, purely staffer-derived and therefore comparable to the bill graph.
- Non-circularity: LobbyView network.csv, lobbyview_network_member.csv, our_network_*.csv and bill_lobbying_sidecar.json are banned as circular. LD-2 filings never name members, so lobbied-member edges are joins by construction; zero influence or predictor phrasing on LDA-derived edges is a language law (I-15). Revolving-layer join on lda_source_person_id verified not circular.
- Inference is never merged with observation: predicted destinations live in a separate exploratory tier, to avoid self-confirmation.
- Identity: STRICT-BIOGUIDE (no fuzzy member joins), declaration-directed matching, paired control arms per widening tier with a positive control, and coverage alarms with match-rate floors that abort fail-closed.

Research questions and syntheses:
- Whether committee payrolls (missed by a prior parse, "committee membership does not exist on disk" was wrong) are the main source of cross-party ties, since personal offices are partisan silos. Overarching argument: the capture pipeline works. Anchor-based capture (a stimulus anchor pad plus manifest offset, and on-screen chyron, and caption text) pins each member's turn exactly (751/751 offsets; padded/unpadded cross-correlation about 1.000 at median lag 20.00s). That yields a ~161-hour, 448-member voice corpus and a 532-of-533-member speech text corpus of about 57.6M words. Transcription (Gemini plus a pinned local Whisper producer) agrees with YouTube captions at 0.945 mean word coverage (n=30 windows), but this is reference-dependent: 0.745 against condensed C-SPAN text, and no human-gold WER exists yet.

Main synthesis: every attempt to validate audio as a Big Five measurement channel missed, was redundant with text, or was confounded. ES held-out r=+0.208 vanished after controls (partial r=-0.029 after gender and party, since pitch encodes speaker sex). E audio-alone r=+0.228 sat inside the permutation noise floor. The N prereg look missed on all four bars (r=-0.0016, n=110), and the channels appear to carry C/E-flavoured signal rather than N. The one partial positive (Pink-E r=+0.284, ES r=+0.298) cannot yield per-trait claims because audio A and ES are halo-inseparable (|r|=0.819). The ruling of record (D-013, 2026-08-25) pivots audio to descriptive, display-only measurement (triggers, speech-habit signatures, agreement/disagreement) with no engine wiring and no trait-validity claims without a fresh locked prereg.

Reliability and venue findings: quirk rates (Spearman-Brown 0.794), pause behavior (0.799 NPR; 0.882 Sunday shows), volume dynamics (0.708) and pitch variability (0.707) clear the 0.70 bar at 5 units. Floor-speech prosody, F0 slopes and vocal strain do not. Filler rates differ roughly 100x between live Washington Journal (~26 per 1k words) and NPR (0.22 per 1k), so raw cross-venue comparisons are invalid.

works.title: Cross Industry Finance and Lobbying Disclosure Report: Analysis and Recommendations
works.summary: Paul's own unpublished client report (to Trey Hawkins and Hannah Benito; year not printed, 2026 inferred) surveys political money in financial services and makes three recommendations to Credit Unions: raise giving 41% over the 2023-2024 baseline to about $4.3M, push employee and middle-management giving to trade groups, and run campaigns that set CUs apart from banks. The extract only covers the Crypto and Community Banks sections. Crypto giving rose from $1.76M (2021-22) to $145.5M (2023-24). The text reports +8,162.6%, but the stated figures give about +8,167%. The C-suite share of that giving went from 69% to 98.8%, and super PACs took 71.9% of non-direct giving, which is itself 70% of the total. A 2025-26 projection of more than $175M would be a midterm-cycle rise, which the report attributes to the CLARITY Act. Crypto-backed candidates won 38 of 40 primaries, and opinion runs 31% oppose to 27% support (no source given). Community-bank member LDA activity rose by an average of 20 interactions. The method is descriptive throughout: no model, no uncertainty, no identification design. Against the system as built, the report matters in three places. (1) Mentat's cycle model applies a symmetric x1.8635 presidential factor to general giving on the midterm step. For a crypto-like industry that projects a large 2025-26 drop, the opposite of the report's projection. (2) The per-member LDA interaction counts look like the bill-roster join that the lobbying lane rejected as circular, and they use LDA as a weight source, which D-021 bars. (3) The super-PAC share and the C-suite share both point to gaps in what Mentat currently splits out. All new analysis here is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

works.title: Request for Review: Industry Economic Performance and Political Spending
works.summary: Paul's September 24, 2026 design memo to a secondary advisor (Astra) asks whether a sector's year-over-year economic performance predicts its federal campaign giving and lobbying, and how expected partisan control shapes the amount and direction of that money. It reports no estimates. It sets out five hypotheses (deep pockets, distress, access-seeking, stakes, lobbying tracks current power) and three pooled sector fixed-effects models. Model 1 is log contributions on prior- and same-year growth together (a distributed lag), a negative-growth dummy, Midterm/Pres, a Tossup term and a trend. Model 2 is Republican two-party share on Shift = P minus RMajNow. Model 3 is log lobbying with a lagged dependent variable and Unified control. Inference is a wild sector-cluster bootstrap with Driscoll-Kraay errors. The proposed panel is 2008-2025 with five sectors, about 9 elections and 6 chamber flips. The memo is the method source for the Mentat sector growth study, and the Codex ORIGINAL_MODEL_CONTRACT transcribes it. The R build diverges from it. Each growth timing enters its own model (C1/C2/C3) rather than one distributed lag. Totals carry a signed exp_dem control where the memo calls for Tossup. There is no negative-growth dummy, trend or lagged lobbying term. The primary window is 2020-2025 (three elections), not 2008-2025. Results so far are null or fragile: no stable partisan shift (-0.04, p .76), and the lobbying growth lead flips sign under year FE. The memo's leverage worries therefore apply to the build with more force. The only within-cycle access-seeking signal, SEATS-W (-3.47 pp per expected D seat, House 2022), comes from one election and uses expected seats, the measure the memo demoted to a robustness check. All agent readings here are UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
works.question: Does a U.S. industry's year-over-year economic performance predict how much it spends on federal politics, through campaign contributions and through lobbying? How does expected partisan control of Congress shape both the amount and the partisan direction of that spending?
works.method: Pooled panel with sector fixed effects, not per-sector regressions. (1) log contributions on prior-year growth, same-year growth, negative-growth dummy, Midterm, Pres, Tossup, trend. (2) RShare by chamber on growth, Shift, RMajNow, Midterm, Pres. (3) log lobbying on lagged log lobbying, growth, Neg, Unified, Midterm, Pres, sample from 2008. Growth is real, z-scored within sector. Robustness: year fixed effects; Shift x RLean; expected seat change. Inference: wild cluster bootstrap by sector; Driscoll-Kraay where year-level terms enter. Forecasts are used only after estimation, to predict 2026.

works.title: Industry Growth and Political Spending: Research Plan
works.summary: Paul's own research plan (dated 2026-09-25) for testing whether industries spend more or less on federal politics when they have grown, are growing, or expect to grow. It specifies OLS with a separate intercept per sector, six core tests (C1-C3 contributions, L1-L3 lobbying, each with prior actual, same-year actual, or IBISWorld predicted growth), election-cycle dummies and IEM expected-control covariates, plus job-tier and per-chamber Democratic-share extensions. Its strongest contributions are discipline rules: predicted growth must come from a report vintage published before the spending year, missing forecasts stay missing, null results are kept, and independent-row OLS errors are ruled insufficient with nine or fewer sector clusters. It reports no estimates, and its own readiness check says contributions overlap the IEM forecasts only in 2021-2022. The document is the north star of the built sector growth study (Mentat sector_growth_study, in R). The build honours the inference caution with a wild cluster restricted bootstrap by sector and Holm adjustment, but departs from the plan in three places: log outcomes rather than dollar levels, a retrospective 2023-2026 expected-control series plus 538 robustness filling the IEM gap, and added Tossup and trend terms. Results recorded in the brain (UNVERIFIED, single path): L3 on LobbyView lobbying b 0.242 million 2025 USD per pp (p 0.033, Holm 0.1125) flips to -0.477 under year FE, growth adds no adjusted R2, and the annual partisan SHIFT is -0.04 (p 0.76). So far the plan's question is answered as no stable growth signal, which bears directly on the live giving forecast that still feeds IBISWorld growth into general giving at 50/50.
works.question: Do industries spend differently on politics (federal campaign contributions and lobbying) when they have grown, are growing, or expect to grow? Does a published industry growth forecast predict subsequent spending, and do expectations about House and Senate control help explain spending?
works.method: Multiple linear regression by OLS with a separate intercept per sector (sector fixed effects). Contributions: Y_it = a_i + b X_it + c Pres_t + d Midterm_t + e ExpectedDemHouse_t + f ExpectedDemSenate_t + error. Lobbying adds CurrentDemHouse_t and CurrentDemSenate_t. X is prior actual growth, same-year actual growth, or predicted growth (tests C1-C3 and L1-L3). Growth in percentage points. Job-tier extension: pooled model with sector-by-tier baselines and growth x tier terms, Employee as reference. Chamber extension: linear model of Democratic share of contributions. Further extensions: prior and predicted growth together; year indicators in place of national controls; logged spending for positive observations. Simple regression only to illustrate scatterplots.

findings.finding: Design is OLS with sector fixed effects and six core tests: C1-C3 explain contributions and L1-L3 explain lobbying, each with prior actual, same-year actual, or predicted growth as the growth regressor.
findings.numbers: 6 core tests; growth in percentage points; spending in millions of 2025 dollars

works.title: Review: industry growth and political spending
works.summary: A design review dated 2026-09-24, filed as Paul's research note, of the Astra brief that became the Mentat sector growth study. It estimates nothing. Its core advice: make prior-year real growth the main question and fit log spending on sector and year fixed effects plus lagged raw percent growth (g(t-1)), separately for organizational PAC giving and LDA lobbying, never summed. Treat election expectations as a separate, exploratory study, because more sectors do not create more elections (about 9 elections, 6 chamber flips). It also says three of the brief's specifications do not test their hypotheses: a contraction dummy is not an asymmetric slope (use g+ and g-); Shift = P - M plus current control only reparameterizes P plus M; and a unified-government term cannot separate expected from current control. On data, it says not to fill missing control probabilities with realized results. It says 538 models that use fundraising create a feedback loop, so a polls-only sensitivity is better. It warns that LDA in-house totals already include retained-firm payments and association dues. With five sectors, it says, use the restricted wild-cluster bootstrap and leave-one-sector-out checks. Against the system as built, several points were adopted: raw percent growth, g_pos/g_neg splits, the restricted wild-cluster bootstrap with a few-cluster guard, LOSO/LOYO, the 538 Lite seat forecasts, and lobbying series that are never summed. Others were not. The primary models use dollar levels with national phase and expected-control controls, and year fixed effects and logs are only robustness checks. The giving outcome is Mentat general giving across all recipient types. The 2023/2025 expected control was filled after the fact by Paul's ruling. The later Codex audit vindicated the review's main warning: the L3-LV lobbying slope of +0.352 flipped to -0.477 under sector and year fixed effects (UNSTRATIFIED, 5 sectors, 2008-2023).
works.question: Does prior-year real industry growth predict subsequent organizational political spending (corporate and trade-association PAC contributions to congressional candidates, and reported LDA lobbying expenditure), and do election expectations (probability of chamber control) predict where PAC giving goes across parties, incumbents and committee members? The growth association is the main question; expectations are a separate, exploratory question.
works.method: Main model: log S_it = alpha_i + lambda_t + beta g_{i,t-1} + e, with sector and year effects, estimated separately for PAC contributions and lobbying (never summed). Growth g = 100 (V_t / V_{t-1} - 1) on raw real value added. Alternatives: PPML exponential conditional mean if genuine zeros exist; log initial sector size at t-2 as a control; split growth into g+ = max(g,0) and g- = max(-g,0) for asymmetry; dynamic FE only as sensitivity (Bruno bias correction; Arellano-Bond or system GMM not recommended with five to ten sectors). Expectations study: RShare = sector/chamber baseline + coefficient times earlier P + coefficient times current control + limited calendar controls, with a fractional-response sensitivity. Inference: small-sample cluster corrections, restricted wild-cluster bootstrap, cluster leverage, leave-one-sector-out, Driscoll-Kraay only as sensitivity, randomization inference only with a defensible assignment argument.

works.title: Sector growth and political spending: source check (START HERE)
works.summary: Paul's September 25, 2026 source check is the data inventory and design note behind the Mentat sector growth study. At that point no regressions had been run. It lists IBISWorld real-revenue growth for four sectors: commercial banks, credit unions, life insurance and auto. It also has a 72-row sector-year panel for 2008-2025, election-year dummies and actual chamber control checked against the House and Senate histories. Expected control (conditional IEM measures) covers 2008-2022 only, and CPI multipliers convert spending to 2025 dollars. The note specifies six core regressions: spending on sector baseline plus growth (same-year, previous-year or predicted), presidential and midterm dummies, and expected Democratic House and Senate control, each run for contributions and lobbying. It also defines a Democratic share by chamber and a Chief / Middle Management / Employee tier split. The built system implements this design almost exactly: sgs_registry.R carries the same three growth variables and the same four controls. The IBISWorld lagged real-growth path also feeds the live giving forecast's 50/50 budget term. The note is now stale. The study has since moved to nine sectors and a 2020-2026 window, and its results are mostly null. Growth adds no adjusted R2 (0.884717 vs 0.884690, LobbyView lobbying). The predicted-growth lobbying coefficient flips from +0.352 to -0.477 under sector and year fixed effects, and its Holm p rises from 0.0375 to 0.1125. The partisan-shift test gives -0.04 (p 0.76, 2021-25). These are agent runs, partly reproduced by a Codex review, so they stay UNVERIFIED under DE-062. The note's warnings still hold: keep blanks as missing, do not deflate IBISWorld twice, and treat expected-control means as concurrent, not causal.
works.question: Does industry revenue growth (same-year or previous-year) predict political spending (campaign contributions and lobbying) by sector, net of presidential and midterm election-year effects and expected congressional control; and does predicted industry growth do the same? Also whether Democratic share of contributions differs by chamber.
works.method: Four actual-growth OLS-style regressions (k=1 previous-year growth; k=0 same-year growth; each for contributions and lobbying): Spending(sector, year) = sector baseline + b x Growth(sector, year-k) + c x PresidentialYear + d x MidtermYear + e x ExpectedDemHouse + f x ExpectedDemSenate + error. Plus two predicted-growth tests using the prior-year forecast for year t in place of actual growth; six core tests total per the linked plan. Party direction: Democratic share = Dem / (Dem + Rep), separately for House and Senate recipients; missing when denominator is zero. Job-level comparison: sector x year x tier (Chief, Middle Management, Employee) for contributions only. No regressions have been run yet.
